Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top- r r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r × r r\times r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiqunMa/ResQAdam .

Quantization-aware training (QAT) inserts the quantizer into the forward pass and updates latent full-precision weights through the straight-through estimator (STE) ( Bengio et al., 2013 ) . At low bit widths it recovers much of the accuracy lost by post-training quantization (PTQ) ( Frantar et al., 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ) , both when fine-tuning a pretrained checkpoint ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) and when training from scratch ( Panferov et al., 2025 ; Tabesh et al., 2025 ) . This accuracy comes at a memory cost. QAT keeps full-precision weights and gradients, and most recipes rely on AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) , which stores two FP32 moments and adds 8 ​ n ​ m 8nm bytes for each n × m n\times m weight matrix. A natural remedy is to borrow memory-efficient optimizers from full-precision training. GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) and LDAdam ( Robert et al., 2024 ) project the gradient onto a rank- r r subspace, keep Adam states only in that subspace, and map the update back to the full space. This works well when the optimization signal is concentrated in a few directions. Figure 1 shows that the same strategy does not carry over to QAT. With rank 64 and tuned learning rates, both methods are clearly worse than AdamW, in from-scratch training as well as in fine-tuning. We hypothesize that this is a property of the QAT update itself. Under the STE, the gradient has to compensate for element-wise quantization errors, which are spread over individual entries rather than aligned with a few directions of the weight matrix. If these corrections are less concentrated in the top- r r subspace than the rest of the update, a projection-based optimizer discards them at every step, and no amount of tuning inside the subspace recovers them.

Figure 1: WikiText-2 perplexity versus optimizer state memory for different optimizers under two QAT paradigms. The x-axis reports the total optimizer state size of the full model (in GB). All experiments use W2A16 quantization with group size 128, and projection-based optimizers use rank 64. For a fair comparison, the learning rate of each optimizer is tuned via grid search and the best result is reported. To address this limitation, we decompose the QAT optimization signal according to its geometric structure. We apply Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to the dense global momentum, retaining the top- r r singular vectors to form the orthonormal bases U t ∈ ℝ n × r U_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} and V t ∈ ℝ m × r V_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} . These bases induce a principal matrix subspace 𝒮 t = { U t ​ A ​ V t ⊤ : A ∈ ℝ r × r } \mathcal{S}_{t}=\left\{U_{t}AV_{t}^{\top}:A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}\right\} . The momentum can then be exactly decomposed into its projection onto 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} and an orthogonal residual lying in 𝒮 t ⟂ \mathcal{S}_{t}^{\perp} . The principal projection captures the dominant low-rank structure of the optimization trajectory, whereas the orthogonal residual retains dispersed signals outside the principal subspace. Our empirical results show that these residual signals become particularly important under QAT. Their magnitude matters little: keeping only their sign, with no second-moment state, recovers most of the lost quality (Section 5.1 ).

Motivated by this insight, we propose ResQAdam ( Res idual-Preserving Q uantization-Aware Adam ), a geometrically decoupled optimizer that applies distinct update rules based on subspace characteristics. It stores one dense momentum in BF16 and refreshes its top- r r singular vectors every τ \tau steps. Adam runs on the r × r r\times r coordinates of the gradient in this subspace, and the residual of the momentum contributes a sign update whose norm matches the Adam update. Since no dense second moment is kept, persistent optimizer memory falls to roughly a quarter of AdamW, and the SVD cost is spread over τ \tau steps. By eliminating dense second-moment tracking, ResQAdam limits the persistent optimizer memory footprint to only the BF16 momentum and negligible low-rank components. For a weight matrix W ∈ ℝ n × m W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} with projection rank r r , the persistent memory ratio compared to standard AdamW is: 2 ​ n ​ m + 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( n + m ) ​ r + r 2 ) / 8 ​ n ​ m ≈ 25 % 2nm+\mathcal{O}((n+m)r+r^{2})/{8nm}\approx 25\% . The measured saving is 71% to 74%. Furthermore, while the required SVD introduces computational overhead, refreshing the bases only once every few hundred steps effectively amortizes this cost, resulting in minimal training-speed degradation.

To evaluate our approach, we conduct extensive experiments across both from-scratch QAT and QAT fine-tuning paradigms. Across multiple LLM architectures, quantization configurations, and QAT methods, our empirical results demonstrate that ResQAdam closely tracks the optimization trajectory and largely preserves AdamW-level final performance across the evaluated settings. It achieves this by reducing around 75% of AdamW’s average memory footprint, while introducing negligible computational overhead for training.

From-scratch QAT. Learnable quantizers such as PACT ( Choi et al., 2018 ) and LSQ ( Esser et al., 2019 ) were later scaled to LLMs by BitNet ( Wang et al., 2023 ) and BitNet b1.58 ( Ma et al., 2024 ) . Recent work improves the gradient estimate. QuEST ( Panferov et al., 2025 ) applies Hadamard transforms and down-weights gradients of entries with large quantization error, and CAGE ( Tabesh et al., 2025 ) adds a curvature-aware correction to the STE. Both quantize only the forward pass and keep gradients and optimizer states in high precision, which is the setting we target. QAT Fine-Tuning. A complementary paradigm adapts a converged full-precision checkpoint to recover its compressed representation. LLM-QAT ( Liu et al., 2024 ) performs data-free QAT by distilling from the pretrained model’s own generations, jointly quantizing weights, activations, and the KV cache. EfficientQAT ( Chen et al., 2025 ) reduces QAT cost via two stages: block-wise all-parameter training (Block-AP) for a strong low-bit initialization, followed by end-to-end training of only the quantization step sizes (E2E-QP). ParetoQ ( Liu et al., 2026 ) unifies 1-to-4-bit QAT under a single framework and identifies a sharp representation transition between 2 and 3 bits. Unlike parameter-efficient alternatives such as PEQA ( Kim et al., 2023 ) , which shrinks optimizer memory by training only the quantization scales, or QLoRA ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) , which fine-tunes high-precision adapters over a frozen quantized base, our method retains full-parameter updates while still reducing optimizer memory. Low-rank projection methods take a different route: GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) periodically computes an SVD of the gradient, runs Adam within the resulting compact subspace, and projects the update back, while LDAdam ( Robert et al., 2024 ) performs adaptive optimization inside dynamically shifting subspaces with a projection-aware transport rule and error feedback. These methods are most effective when optimization signals are strongly concentrated in a dominant low-rank subspace. Our experiments show that this assumption becomes substantially less effective under QAT: projection-only optimizers degrade markedly, while preserving the discarded residual restores much of the lost optimization quality. While recent works like Fira ( Chen et al., 2026 ) and FRUGAL ( Zmushko et al., 2024 ) also update the component outside the projected subspace with a state-free rule. ResQAdam differs in the residual is taken from the momentum rather than the current gradient, the bases are computed from the momentum, and the two updates are weighted by their momentum energy.

Based on the explicit orthogonal decomposition of optimization signals, we propose ResQAdam, a geometrically decoupled optimizer for QAT. ResQAdam applies different update rules to two parts of the optimization space: a compact coordinate space in ℝ r × r \mathbb{R}^{r\times r} , where Adam-style preconditioning is performed, and the full parameter space ℝ n × m \mathbb{R}^{n\times m} , where the orthogonal residual provides a sign-based correction for dispersed quantization-compensation signals. This decomposition substantially reduces the optimizer memory footprint while retaining the residual correction signals required for QAT. The overall training flow is summarized in Algorithm 2 .

From-scratch QAT. We consider QuEST ( Panferov et al., 2025 ) and CAGE ( Tabesh et al., 2025 ) , which represent two recent low-precision training frameworks with distinct gradient-estimation and optimization strategies. We pretrain Llama-style models at the 200M and 430M scales under W2A2, W2A16, and W4A4 settings. QAT fine-tuning. Optimization Trajectory and Convergence Alignment. As illustrated in Figure 2 , ResQAdam closely tracks the training-loss trajectory of the dense AdamW baseline. Across all evaluated bit-width configurations and both frameworks, the training loss curves of ResQAdam closely overlap with the baseline from initialization through to the final iterations. The zoomed-in callouts at the end of the training horizons further highlight that ResQAdam maintains stable convergence without divergence. This confirms that our geometry-decoupled and space-specific update strategies sufficiently capture the quantization errors to stabilize the low-bit pretraining process. Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

Table 2 compares ResQAdam with AdamW across the three fine-tuning recipes, which differ in data source, training objective and optimization granularity. Across these settings, ResQAdam generally achieves performance close to AdamW in both perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, while reducing optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74%. Although some aggressive W2A16 block-wise settings show larger metric fluctuations, the overall results indicate that ResQAdam can serve as a memory-efficient alternative to AdamW for diverse QAT fine-tuning pipelines.

We ablate the main components of ResQAdam on a 297M model under W2A2, W2A16, and W4A4 from-scratch QAT. To keep the ablation aligned with the goal of memory-efficient QAT, we restrict the comparison to lightweight variants that do not introduce substantial extra computation or optimizer-state memory. Variants whose added cost would eliminate the memory or throughput advantage over AdamW are excluded, since they would not be practical alternatives to AdamW. Principal Update Only: Uses only the Adam-preconditioned update in the principal subspace, i.e., Δ t = Δ t ∥ \Delta_{t}=\Delta_{t}^{\parallel} , and removes the sign correction from the orthogonal residual. Residual-Sign Only: Uses only the normalized sign direction derived from the orthogonal residual M t ⟂ M_{t}^{\perp} , and removes the Adam-preconditioned principal update. Gradient-SVD Bases: Computes the projection bases U t , V t U_{t},V_{t} from the instantaneous gradient G t G_{t} instead of the momentum M t M_{t} , while keeping the remaining update rule unchanged. Global-Momentum Sign: Applies a sign update directly to the momentum M t M_{t} without decomposing it into the principal component and the orthogonal residual. ResQAdam: Uses the full design: Adam-style preconditioning in the r × r r\times r coordinate representation, residual-sign correction from M t ⟂ M_{t}^{\perp} , and momentum energy-weighting to fuse the two updates. Figure 3 reports the average perplexity on C4 and WikiText-2. The Principal Update Only variant performs poorly across all quantization settings, showing that updates restricted to the principal subspace are not sufficient for QAT. The Residual-Sign Only variant performs much better, especially under W2A2 and W2A16, which indicates that the orthogonal residual contains useful correction signals. However, it is not consistently better than the full method, suggesting that the Adam-preconditioned principal update still provides important low-rank structural information. The Gradient-SVD Bases variant underperforms ResQAdam, particularly under W2A2, validating the extraction of projection bases from the time-smoothed momentum rather than instantaneous gradients. Similarly, the Global-Momentum Sign variant falls short, demonstrating that applying a monolithic sign update negates the benefits of separating the principal component from the residual. Overall, the full ResQAdam consistently achieves the best perplexity across the evaluated settings, supporting the effectiveness of combining principal-subspace Adam preconditioning with a residual-derived sign correction.

chunks.text: Figure 4: Sensitivity of ResQAdam to the rank r r and the SVD refresh interval τ \tau on a 297M model trained from scratch. The y-axis is the average of WikiText-2 and C4 perplexity. Figure 5: Energy ratio of the principal subspace ( ρ t ∥ \rho_{t}^{\parallel} ) during from-scratch QAT on a 297M Llama-style model. The curves represent different weight matrices within a middle transformer layer across W2A16, W4A4, and W2A2 quantization configurations.

We track the energy ratio of the principal subspace, ρ t ∥ = ‖ M t ∥ ‖ F / ( ‖ M t ‖ F + ϵ ) \rho_{t}^{\parallel}=\|M_{t}^{\parallel}\|_{F}/(\|M_{t}\|_{F}+\epsilon) , for the seven weight matrices of a middle layer in the 297M model pretrained with ResQAdam. We record it only at refresh steps, right after the bases are recomputed from M t M_{t} . At these points ρ t ∥ \rho_{t}^{\parallel} is at its highest, so any residual energy we observe is a lower bound on the energy that a projection-based optimizer discards during the following τ \tau steps. The result is shown in Figure 5 . ρ t ∥ \rho_{t}^{\parallel} starts high, decreases, and settles at a level that depends on the matrix. It remains relatively high for attention K and V and is lowest for the MLP down projection, while the bit-width setting has a smaller effect. Even immediately after a refresh, a substantial share of the momentum lies outside 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} , and projection-based optimizers discard this share. Overall, the principal subspace consistently captures a meaningful but incomplete fraction of the momentum. This supports ResQAdam’s selective-adaptivity design: Adam-style preconditioning is beneficial for the structured principal component, while a full-space residual correction remains necessary to preserve the substantial optimization signal outside the low-rank subspace.

In this paper, we proposed ResQAdam, a memory-efficient optimizer tailored for LLM QAT. We demonstrated that standard low-rank optimizers struggle in QAT because they discard important residual optimization signals outside the dominant principal subspace. ResQAdam leveraged Adam within this subspace and adds a sign update from the residual. Extensive experiments across from-scratch QAT and fine-tuning show that ResQAdam closely tracks AdamW’s convergence behavior and largely preserves its final performance, while reducing persistent optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74%, respectively.

chunks.section: Appendix A Estimating the Statistics of Projected Gradients
chunks.text: When the projection bases are refreshed, the coordinate representation of the principal subspace changes from ( U t − 1 , V t − 1 ) (U_{t-1},V_{t-1}) to ( U t , V t ) (U_{t},V_{t}) , where t − 1 t-1 denotes the last step before the refresh. Since Adam-style preconditioning is anisotropic, directly reusing the old principal moments m t − 1 ∥ m_{t-1}^{\parallel} and v t − 1 ∥ v_{t-1}^{\parallel} in the new coordinate system would mix statistics computed under different bases. To address this, we adopt the statistical state transport mechanism introduced by LDAdam ( Robert et al., 2024 ) , which estimates the first- and second-order statistics of the newly projected gradients. As noted in Section 3.4 , only the compact principal states are transported. We treat this transport as a lightweight heuristic that maintains the continuity of the Adam-preconditioned principal update across refreshes. Recall that ResQAdam projects the full-space gradient G t ∈ ℝ n × m G_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} into the r × r r\times r coordinate representation of the principal subspace as G t ∥ = U t ⊤ ​ G t ​ V t ∈ ℝ r × r . G_{t}^{\parallel}=U_{t}^{\top}G_{t}V_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}. (8) Let the old and new bases define the transition matrices P t = U t ⊤ ​ U t − 1 ∈ ℝ r × r , Q t = V t − 1 ⊤ ​ V t ∈ ℝ r × r . P_{t}=U_{t}^{\top}U_{t-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r},\qquad Q_{t}=V_{t-1}^{\top}V_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}. (9) Under the rank- r r truncation induced by the old bases, the projection of any past gradient G k G_{k} ( k < t k<t ) into the new coordinate representation can be approximated by

While the statistical transport equations strictly follow LDAdam ( Robert et al., 2024 ) , our application differs in scope. LDAdam relies on this transport to perform adaptive optimization entirely within the compressed principal subspace, using generalized error feedback to reintroduce projection errors. In contrast, ResQAdam restricts this transport solely to the compact principal states m t ∥ , v t ∥ ∈ ℝ r × r m_{t}^{\parallel},v_{t}^{\parallel}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r} . We maintain a dense momentum M t M_{t} in the original parameter space (stored in BF16) and explicitly preserve the discarded orthogonal residual M t ⟂ M_{t}^{\perp} through a full-space sign correction. Thus, our use of the projected-gradient statistic estimation serves purely as a continuity mechanism for the principal update, deliberately avoiding the compression of residual QAT compensations into LDAdam-style dense second-moment tracking.

chunks.section: Appendix C QAT Frameworks and Experimental Configurations
chunks.text: We evaluate ResQAdam across both from-scratch QAT and post-pretraining QAT fine-tuning, covering substantially different optimization objectives, training schemes, and quantization settings.
We consider two recent low-precision pretraining frameworks.

QuEST ( Panferov et al., 2025 ) applies Hadamard transformations to weights and activations before quantization and uses a trust-based gradient estimator to reduce gradient bias from large quantization errors. We replace its original optimizer with ResQAdam while keeping the remaining training pipeline unchanged.

CAGE ( Tabesh et al., 2025 ) augments the STE with a curvature-aware correction derived from a multi-objective formulation that jointly considers task loss and quantization error. ResQAdam is integrated without modifying its quantization or gradient-correction scheme. For both frameworks, we pretrain Llama-style models with 200M and 430M parameters on C4 under W2A2, W2A16, and W4A4 quantization. The training-token budget is set to 40 × 40\times the model size.
We further evaluate ResQAdam under three QAT fine-tuning frameworks with different optimization objectives and data sources.

Our Basic QAT baseline performs end-to-end next-token training with learnable asymmetric quantization, where quantization scales are optimized following LSQ ( Esser et al., 2019 ) . All parameters are jointly fine-tuned on a 2B-token subset of RedPajama ( Computer, 2023 ) .

EfficientQAT ( Chen et al., 2025 ) first performs block-wise all-parameter training (Block-AP), followed by an E2E-QP stage that updates only quantization parameters. Since ResQAdam operates on weight-matrix updates, we evaluate it only in the Block-AP stage.

LLM-QAT ( Liu et al., 2024 ) uses data-free knowledge distillation, generating training sequences from the full-precision teacher and optimizing the quantized student to match it. It jointly quantizes weights, activations, and the KV cache using symmetric MinMax quantization. For fine-tuning experiments, we use Llama 3.2-1B ( AI@Meta, 2024 ) , Qwen 3-4B-Base ( Team, 2025 ) , and Llama 2-7B ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) under multiple low-bit quantization configurations. Exact configurations are reported with the corresponding experimental results.
